top_choice_rationale: Mircea Cărtărescu (P002) best meets the criterion I put first, a voice found in this writer's work and nowhere else. From public descriptions, Blinding and Solenoid turn memory, the body and dream into one sustained metaphysical project. That voice is recognisable at the level of the sentence and of the whole structure. Solenoid's anchoring in an ordinary bodily life supplies the human dimension the case needs. The citation is confined to the prose, because the poetry is the least accessible part of the corpus in translation. This is a provisional judgement. I cannot verify whether the late volumes keep their emotional and moral range or only extend structure, and the density of the Romanian prose may not survive translation. I put Adonis (P001) a close second. A language-level renewal is a serious and durable kind of distinctiveness, and I cannot show it is weaker than an architecture of prose. My preference rests on what I can assess under uncertainty, not on demonstrated greater merit. If the late Cărtărescu volumes only repeat their design, Adonis would move first for me. Carson (P003) ranks third. Her formal invention is real, but the evidence for breadth across the oeuvre is thinner than for the other two. P000 ranks last, because translation limits apply to every candidate and do not justify withholding the prize.
